title: Tracking What Crosses a Membrane
endLine: Measure transport across sealed membranes, then test one purified protein alone.

scenes.tts: Why does water cross a bare lipid bilayer about ten billion times faster than smaller sodium? Sodium is about one point zero angstroms in radius; water is about one point four angstroms. How do scientists prove which protein moves an ion across?
scenes.caption: Why does water cross a bare lipid bilayer about ten billion times faster than smaller sodium? Sodium is about 1.0 Å in radius; water is about 1.4 Å. How do scientists prove which protein moves an ion across?
scenes.visual: Cross-section of a bare lipid bilayer (two simple geometric leaflets, no molecular structures) filling 65% of frame height, separating outer bath from inner fluid. A smaller bright sodium dot labelled 'Na+ ~1.0 Å' bounces repeatedly off the bilayer while a larger blue water dot labelled 'Water ~1.4 Å' slips across. A bold bar on the right ('schematic') shows water crossing ~10 billion times faster. On the final question, an empty glowing slot pulses in the bilayer with a question mark.
scenes.narration: Why does water cross a bare lipid bilayer about ten billion times faster than smaller sodium? Sodium is about 1.0 Å in radius; water is about 1.4 Å. How do scientists prove which protein moves an ion across?

scenes.tts: Sodium loses because a bilayer has an oily core. Gases like oxygen cross by simple diffusion. Leaving water for oil costs ions and sugars too much energy. So cells build specific proteins. To measure transport, scientists follow tracers, detectable labelled copies of a solute, across sealed membranes.
scenes.caption: Sodium loses because a bilayer has an oily core. Gases like oxygen cross by simple diffusion. Leaving water for oil costs ions and sugars too much energy. So cells build specific proteins. To measure transport, scientists follow tracers, detectable labelled copies of a solute, across sealed membranes.
scenes.visual: Same bilayer cross-section; its middle band glows warm amber labelled 'Oily core' as small oxygen dots drift across while sodium and glucose dots recoil ('schematic'). A simple geometric protein block slides into the empty slot in the bilayer, opening a path. Glowing tracer dots gather outside as the flat bilayer smoothly curves into a closed ring, forming the carried vesicle world.
scenes.narration: Sodium loses because a bilayer has an oily core. Gases like oxygen cross by simple diffusion. Leaving water for oil costs ions and sugars too much energy. So cells build specific proteins. To measure transport, scientists follow tracers, detectable labelled copies of a solute, across sealed membranes.

scenes.tts: First, researchers isolate vesicles: small, sealed bubbles of membrane enclosing fluid. They add a tracked solute outside, plus any fuel a pump needs, such as A T P. When transport runs, solute leaves the surrounding fluid and builds up inside.
scenes.caption: First, researchers isolate vesicles: small, sealed bubbles of membrane enclosing fluid. They add a tracked solute outside, plus any fuel a pump needs, such as ATP. When transport runs, solute leaves the surrounding fluid and builds up inside.
scenes.visual: The curved bilayer finishes closing into one large sealed vesicle ('Vesicle', filling 65% of frame height) in a bath, with a schematic pump block embedded in its wall and a two-bar gauge ('Outside' vs 'Inside', labelled 'schematic') on the right. Glowing solute dots appear outside alongside small ATP tokens. As ATP tokens dock at the pump, solute dots cross inward; the 'Outside' bar falls while the 'Inside' bar rises.
scenes.narration: First, researchers isolate vesicles: small, sealed bubbles of membrane enclosing fluid. They add a tracked solute outside, plus any fuel a pump needs, such as ATP. When transport runs, solute leaves the surrounding fluid and builds up inside.

scenes.tts: Yet a cell vesicle still holds many proteins. To test one candidate alone, scientists purify it. They place it into bare liposomes, synthetic lipid bubbles, or an insensitive cell.
scenes.caption: Yet a cell vesicle still holds many proteins. To test one candidate alone, scientists purify it. They place it into bare liposomes, synthetic lipid bubbles, or an insensitive cell.
scenes.visual: The carried vesicle's rim reveals several different grey schematic protein blocks alongside one bright teal candidate protein. The teal block lifts out as the cluttered vesicle fades into a clean empty lipid ring labelled 'Liposome' ('schematic'). The single purified teal block inserts into the bare liposome wall while solute dots wait outside.
scenes.narration: Yet a cell vesicle still holds many proteins. To test one candidate alone, scientists purify it. They place it into bare liposomes, synthetic lipid bubbles, or an insensitive cell.

scenes.tts: Pause and predict. You purify a candidate protein and place it into bare liposomes. You add the solute outside, and nothing crosses the membrane. Does that prove you chose the wrong protein?
scenes.caption: Pause and predict. You purify a candidate protein and place it into bare liposomes. You add the solute outside, and nothing crosses the membrane. Does that prove you chose the wrong protein?
scenes.visual: The carried bare liposome sits centred with the single teal protein embedded in its wall. Bright solute dots drift slowly in the outer bath; none cross inward, and the 'Inside' gauge stays flat at zero ('schematic'). Large high-contrast text appears above: 'Nothing crosses — wrong protein?'
scenes.narration: Pause and predict. You purify a candidate protein and place it into bare liposomes. You add the solute outside, and nothing crosses the membrane. Does that prove you chose the wrong protein?

scenes.visual: Hold the same liposome frame for a 4.5-second thinking pause. The question 'Nothing crosses — wrong protein?' stays bold on screen while outer solute dots drift gently in slow ambient motion and the 'Inside' gauge stays flat at zero.

scenes.tts: Not necessarily. A failure in a bare bilayer may only mean a missing partner protein. Orientation matters too: a pump placed backward pushes the wrong way. And a channel or passive carrier moves solute only downhill, so without a concentration or voltage push, nothing crosses.
scenes.caption: Not necessarily. A failure in a bare bilayer may only mean a missing partner protein. Orientation matters too: a pump placed backward pushes the wrong way. And a channel or passive carrier moves solute only downhill, so without a concentration or voltage push, nothing crosses.
scenes.visual: The question clears to 'Not necessarily.' On the carried liposome wall, three sequential transformations animate in place ('schematic'): first, a second partner block docks beside the teal protein and a dot crosses; next, the pump flips upside down with its arrow reversing outward; finally, a passive channel opens only when the outer bath shows a downhill concentration and voltage push.
scenes.narration: Not necessarily. A failure in a bare bilayer may only mean a missing partner protein. Orientation matters too: a pump placed backward pushes the wrong way. And a channel or passive carrier moves solute only downhill, so without a concentration or voltage push, nothing crosses.

scenes.tts: Controls also guard against false positives. Protein-free liposomes measure background leak across bare lipids alone. Without an intact seal, a pump cannot hold a gradient. In a cell sheet, tight seals similarly limit what slips between neighbours and leaks back.
scenes.caption: Controls also guard against false positives. Protein-free liposomes measure background leak across bare lipids alone. Without an intact seal, a pump cannot hold a gradient. In a cell sheet, tight seals similarly limit what slips between neighbours and leaks back.
scenes.visual: Beside the carried liposome, an empty lipid ring labelled 'No protein' shows a tiny background trickle of dots ('schematic'). A gap opens in the liposome wall and built-up inner dots spill out as the 'Inside' gauge drops. The ring briefly transforms into two neighbouring cells joined by a bright clasp labelled 'Tight seal' that blocks dots from slipping between them.
scenes.narration: Controls also guard against false positives. Protein-free liposomes measure background leak across bare lipids alone. Without an intact seal, a pump cannot hold a gradient. In a cell sheet, tight seals similarly limit what slips between neighbours and leaks back.

scenes.tts: Another check asks whether an enzyme sits inside sealed vesicles rather than stuck outside. Detergent opens membranes its substrate cannot cross. Suppose intact vesicles show ten percent of the activity, and detergent raises it to one hundred. Hidden equals total minus intact: one hundred minus ten leaves ninety percent inside.
scenes.caption: Another check asks whether an enzyme sits inside sealed vesicles rather than stuck outside. Detergent opens membranes its substrate cannot cross. Suppose intact vesicles show 10% of the activity, and detergent raises it to 100%. Hidden equals total minus intact: 100% minus 10% leaves 90% inside.
scenes.visual: Return to one intact carried vesicle with schematic enzyme markers enclosed inside and blocked substrate dots bouncing off the intact rim; the gauge reads '10% intact'. Detergent droplets open gaps in the ring; substrate floods inside and the gauge climbs to '100% + detergent'. Beside the gauge, the formula appears step by step as spoken: 'Hidden = Total - Intact', then '100% - 10% = 90% inside' (computed from the lesson example).
scenes.narration: Another check asks whether an enzyme sits inside sealed vesicles rather than stuck outside. Detergent opens membranes its substrate cannot cross. Suppose intact vesicles show 10% of the activity, and detergent raises it to 100%. Hidden equals total minus intact: 100% minus 10% leaves 90% inside.

scenes.tts: These assays unlocked how cells pay for transport. In 1961, Wilhelm Hasselbach and Madoka Makinose added A T P to isolated muscle vesicles. Calcium left the surrounding fluid. Setsuro Ebashi and Fritz Lipmann independently reported A T P-driven uptake in 1962. The cost was about two calcium ions per A T P split.
scenes.caption: These assays unlocked how cells pay for transport. In 1961, Wilhelm Hasselbach and Madoka Makinose added ATP to isolated muscle vesicles. Calcium left the surrounding fluid. Setsuro Ebashi and Fritz Lipmann independently reported ATP-driven uptake in 1962. The cost was about two calcium ions per ATP split.
scenes.visual: The carried vesicle is tagged 'Muscle vesicles · 1961–1962'. One ATP token docks at the schematic pump and two glowing calcium dots move from the outer bath into the lumen; the outer bath dims while the inner bar ticks up with a bold ratio tag '2 Ca2+ per ATP' (from lesson values; pump geometry schematic).
scenes.narration: These assays unlocked how cells pay for transport. In 1961, Wilhelm Hasselbach and Madoka Makinose added ATP to isolated muscle vesicles. Calcium left the surrounding fluid. Setsuro Ebashi and Fritz Lipmann independently reported ATP-driven uptake in 1962. The cost was about two calcium ions per ATP split.

scenes.tts: Expressed in frog oocytes, large egg cells, human S G L T one moves two sodium ions per sugar. Purified rat channel T R P V one was placed in liposomes. After a rapid heat jump, its current rose on a time scale of about three point five milliseconds. Isolating membranes and testing purified proteins turns a crowded cell into clear proof.
scenes.caption: Expressed in frog oocytes, large egg cells, human SGLT1 moves two sodium ions per sugar. Purified rat channel TRPV1 was placed in liposomes. After a rapid heat jump, its current rose on a time scale of about 3.5 ms. Isolating membranes and testing purified proteins turns a crowded cell into clear proof.
scenes.visual: The carried membrane transforms twice in place ('schematic' except quoted values): first into a frog oocyte membrane where a schematic SGLT1 block moves two sodium dots with one sugar dot ('2 Na+ : 1 sugar'); then back into a bare liposome holding one schematic TRPV1 channel as a warm heat sweep triggers a fast current rise labelled '~3.5 ms'. The frame settles on a clean glowing liposome with one protein.
scenes.narration: Expressed in frog oocytes, large egg cells, human SGLT1 moves two sodium ions per sugar. Purified rat channel TRPV1 was placed in liposomes. After a rapid heat jump, its current rose on a time scale of about 3.5 ms. Isolating membranes and testing purified proteins turns a crowded cell into clear proof.
